title: Old quadrille orchestrations and copyrighting his arrangement
summary: They discuss lost quadrille orchestrations and sheet music, and copyrighting his own arrangement when composers were unknown.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: He's a pretty good clarinet player too. I have some of the old piano, the sheet music to some of the old quadrilles that I pick up now and then. But I never did get any orchestrations of them. No, that's what I'm telling you. The orchestrations were gone. At one time did they sell the orchestrations too? Was I? At one time when you were young, did they have the orchestrations for sang-al-tino on those quadrilles?

Yeah, yeah, yeah. They didn't buy all of them. Yeah, but it's all out of date. It's always way past the, it's way past the public domain as the copyright. That's right, the expired domain. And I even, in copywriting it, I even had to tell the copyright officers, of course, they ask you who were the composers, and who was the artist and so forth. I had to tell them I didn't even know who the composers were. And I don't even remember seeing the music, looking at the music itself. But it was just that I remembered the area and I placed my own arrangement.
Yes, you can always copyright your own arrangement, of course.
